newsitem.title: USA: White House, airlines modify airport bag matching.
newsitem.headline: White House, airlines modify airport bag matching.

text.p: The White House aviation safety panel and airlines have agreed to modify a timetable for matching passengers and bags in order to avoid feared airport congestion and flight delays, airlines said on Friday.
The Aviation Safety and Security commission, headed by Vice President Al Gore, recommended on September 9 that at least one hub airport try a full bag match within 60 days.

But airlines said an untested trial to assure a potential terrorist did not check a bag with a bomb and then not board the plane himself would create massive disruptions not only at the test airport but at connecting airports as well.

A senior official of the Air Transport Association, the trade group of the major U.S. carriers, said the two sides agreed after a meeting to run computer tests on bag matching before a bag match was actually run at any airport.
John Meenan, ATA vice president for policy and planning, said the commission recognized the potential problems of a bag match without any prior testing.
There was no immediate comment from the commission.
Meenan said that with a full bag match, aviation would grind to a near halt -- "bags would be lined up on runways. Thousands of passengers delayed."
He added: "We don't believe that is what the commission desired."

Some industry officials have questioned bag matching for domestic travel, saying it could cause massive airport snarls and require costly airport expansions to handle the thousands of passengers requied to wait for bags to be matched.

Meenan said bags are matched on international flights, but under different circumstances -- passengers are required to show up at least 90 minutes before departure and there are few international hubs where departure schedules in one city are timed to mesh to arrivals and depatures in others.
The commission was formed by President Clinton after the July 17 crash of Trans World Airlines flight 800 off Long Island, killing all 230 people on board.
No cause has yet been determined, but investigators say that a bomb placed aboard the Boeing 747 is a possibility.
The commission also recommended increased bag inspections by bomb detecting machines and wider use of bomb-sniffing dogs, well as tighter security checks for airport employees.

Meenan said the computer testing would include determining the number of bags that might have to be pulled from a flight, the time to take bags off the plane, inspecting them and then returing the matched bags.
It could take 45-60 minutes to pull bags out of a plane and to return them, not only holding up that flight, and its gate, but also delaying other flights in connecting cities.
